opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different pieces to break apart here.

On pretraining, my sense is that we've seen somewhat diminishing returns relative to what people expected a few years ago. There's been a lot of discussion about whether we've "hit a wall," and I don't think that's quite right. It's more that the low-hanging fruit of scaling up compute on internet text has been picked to a greater extent, and data constraints are starting to bite somewhat. You can still get gains from bigger pretraining runs, but each order of magnitude seems to buy you a bit less in terms of the capabilities people care about, especially the agentic, long-horizon stuff. And compute scaling itself can't continue at the historical rate forever. At some point you run into constraints on chips, power, and just how much money people are willing to spend, probably sometime around the end of the decade if trends continue.

RL is where I think a lot of the action is right now. The recent jump in reasoning models came largely from doing RL on top of a strong pretrained base, especially in domains where you can check answers, like math and coding. What's notable is that RL compute has been scaled up from a pretty small base, so there's been a lot of room to grow quickly. The big open question is how well that generalizes. Does RL on verifiable tasks transfer to messier, harder-to-check tasks? Can we build good enough environments and reward signals for things like long software engineering projects or research? My guess is that it transfers partially, and that companies will put enormous effort into building richer RL environments, so we'll keep seeing fairly fast progress in the domains that matter most for automating AI R&D, which is the thing I care most about.

If I try to put it together: I don't think scaling is going to stall out in the next couple of years. I expect continued substantial progress, particularly in software and agentic tasks, where the time horizon of tasks AIs can do autonomously has been doubling pretty quickly. But I'm uncertain whether current approaches get us all the way to AIs that can fully automate AI research, or whether we hit a slower regime where progress depends more on algorithmic breakthroughs. I'd put meaningful probability on very capable systems around the end of the decade, and also meaningful probability on things taking a good deal longer, partly because compute scaling has to slow down at some point. That uncertainty is a big part of why I think it's worth preparing seriously now rather than waiting to see.

r001.rationale: It says larger pretraining runs can still produce gains, but does not suggest adapting training methods to larger compute budgets to increase pretraining returns.

r002.rationale: It identifies RL as a major source of progress, noting that RL compute has room to grow and may continue driving gains even as pretraining returns diminish.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate comparing future cluster capacity with the speculated DeepSeek-R1 RL-compute budget.

r004.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about how well RL generalizes, but does not suggest RL may hit diminishing returns because it has elicited most latent model capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd break this down is to look at the two main inputs separately and then think about how they compound.

On pretraining: the basic story is that you get maybe three to four orders of magnitude of additional effective compute scaling over the next several years if trends continue. Training runs have been going up by something like 4 to 5x per year in raw compute, plus you get algorithmic improvements on top of that, which have historically been worth maybe another 2 or 3x per year. So if you just extrapolate, you're looking at models that are trained with something like 1,000 to 10,000 times the effective compute of GPT-4 by the end of the decade. That's a lot. The GPT-3 to GPT-4 jump was roughly two orders of magnitude of effective compute, and that was a pretty dramatic qualitative change. So I don't think we should expect pretraining scaling to just stop yielding gains.

That said, there are real questions. One is data: we're running into limits on high-quality natural text, and it's unclear how much synthetic data or multimodal data substitutes. Another is that the returns look fairly smooth in loss but maybe lumpy in capabilities, and it's hard to predict exactly which capabilities show up when. And there's a more pessimistic view, which I take somewhat seriously, that the returns to pure pretraining have been slowing in a way that's not fully explained by labs holding back.

The thing that I think changes the picture a lot is RL. What we've seen with reasoning models is that you can take a pretrained base and apply reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable outcomes, math, code, agentic tasks, and get very large improvements for relatively small amounts of compute. And critically, the amount of compute going into RL has so far been tiny relative to pretraining. So there's a lot of room to scale that up. If you believe that RL compute can be scaled up by a couple orders of magnitude and that the gains continue roughly as they have, that's a pretty big deal on its own, independent of pretraining.

The uncertainty there is generalization. RL works really cleanly when you have a reward signal you can check, and it's less clear how much it transfers to messy, long-horizon, open-ended tasks where there isn't a crisp success criterion. My current guess is that it transfers more than skeptics think but less than optimists hope, and that a lot of the action in the next few years is going to be about constructing environments and reward signals for progressively harder and less well-specified tasks.

So putting it together: I'd say I'm fairly confident we get substantial gains from continuing to scale both, probably enough to get to systems that are meaningfully better than current ones at agentic software engineering and research-like tasks. Whether that gets you all the way to AI that can fully automate AI research, which is the thing I care most about, is much less certain. I put maybe something like 25% on that happening by 2029 and something like 50% by the mid-2030s, with a lot of the probability mass concentrated on the scenario where RL scaling plus continued pretraining growth just kind of works without needing any major new paradigm.

r002.rationale: It says scaling RL could produce substantial gains and calls those gains a big deal “independent of pretraining,” including if pure pretraining returns are slowing.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate comparing future cluster capacity with a speculated DeepSeek-R1 RL compute budget.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: how much improvement we should expect from scaling pretraining, and how much reinforcement learning can add on top of that.

For pretraining, my basic expectation is that more compute will continue to improve capabilities, but there’s substantial uncertainty about how useful those improvements will be. You can get fairly predictable improvements in prediction loss without getting equally predictable improvements in the particular tasks you care about. Data availability and the quality of the data also matter, so I wouldn’t assume that you can just keep running the same recipe at larger scales indefinitely.

Reinforcement learning potentially gives you another substantial source of gains, especially on tasks where you can reliably check whether an answer is correct. You can have the model try different approaches and reinforce the ones that work. That seems particularly promising for things like programming and mathematics. The harder question is how well those gains generalise to tasks where success is difficult to measure, or where feedback takes a long time to arrive.

And these aren’t independent. A stronger pretrained model might be much better at discovering useful strategies during reinforcement learning. Conversely, if the model almost never succeeds at a task, getting a useful learning signal can be difficult.

So I think there’s a reasonable case for substantial further capability gains. But I’m much less confident about the rate, or about how smoothly those gains translate into being able to do long, complicated tasks autonomously. That’s the distinction I’d want to keep track of: getting better at individual problems versus reliably doing an entire project.

r002.rationale: It presents reinforcement learning as another source of gains, but does not say this could help even if pretraining has diminishing returns.

r003.rationale: The response gives no estimate comparing future cluster compute with a speculated DeepSeek-R1 reinforcement-learning budget.

r004.rationale: It notes that sparse success can make reinforcement-learning feedback difficult, but does not propose diminishing returns from already eliciting most of a model’s latent capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate those two somewhat. For pretraining, I think there’s still a pretty strong case that spending more compute gets you more capable models. The uncertainty is how much more useful capability you get, and whether you run into constraints around data or the cost of doing the next big training run. Smooth improvements in prediction loss don’t necessarily tell you exactly when a model will become good at some economically important task.

Reinforcement learning seems like a potentially substantial additional source of gains, particularly in domains where you can check whether an answer is correct, like coding or maths. You can have the model try things, get feedback, and learn to do better. And that might also teach it to use more computation effectively when solving a problem.

But there’s an important uncertainty about how broadly that generalises. Getting very good at tasks with clean, automatically checkable rewards isn’t necessarily the same as getting good at long, messy projects where success is hard to evaluate. You need the training process to reward actually doing the thing you want.

So I’d expect meaningful further gains from both. I’m less confident about the rate, and especially about whether those gains will be enough to automate AI research. That’s a particularly important threshold, because then improvements in capability could themselves accelerate the process of making better AI systems.
